一弦琴起源於南亞次大陸，特別是在孟加拉地區的Baul民族傳統中發展而來。作為一種: The ektara originated in the South Asian subcontinent, developing in particular within the Baul tradition of Bengal. As an old folk instrument it carries the deep cultural grounding and musical tradition of Bengal. Its design is simple: a gourd serves as the resonator, covered with skin, with a bamboo neck passing through it, showing the ingenuity of early South Asian instrument making.
一弦琴音色溫潤而略帶滄桑感，具有獨特的民族風味。其聲音呈現中等亮度，兼具溫暖與蒼: The ektara's tone is warm with a hint of wear, and has a flavour all its own. It sits at medium brightness, at once warm and bleak, with a slight nasal quality. Because it has a single string its range is fairly limited, mostly from the middle to the upper middle. The gourd resonator covered with skin gives a mild resonance that wraps the tone softly, unlike the bright plucked instruments. Beside the Western guitar the ektara sounds plainer and more inward; beside the Indian sitar it has less of the showy bending and more direct human feeling. Its sound suits narrative folk melody and is very expressive.

The tuntina (ektara) is a chordophone used in Bengal, eastern India and Nepal in South Asia, a drone lute. It is built from a skin-covered gourd resonator with a bamboo neck pushed into it, and a single string runs from the peg to the sounding face and is plucked with the index finger; the player holds the neck, and pressing its two sides changes the string tension and lowers the pitch, producing a drone accompaniment. The two-string version is called the dotara. It is common in Baul music, kirtan singing and Sufi recitation, and is also used by yogis and wandering holy men for singing and prayer, while in Nepal it accompanies recitations of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.
它主要作為人聲伴奏出現於孟加拉傳統音樂、現代孟加拉與印度東部音樂，以及巴烏爾音樂: It appears mainly as an accompaniment to the voice, in traditional Bengali music, in modern Bengali and eastern Indian music, and in Baul music; it is also used for the singing and prayer of yogis and wandering holy men, and in Nepal it accompanies recitations of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. It is common besides in kirtan and Sufi singing, where its drone supports call-and-response singing, or in dance where it keeps time with hand cymbals. In recent years it has also appeared in Bengali pop bands and films, mixed with modern sounds.
此類單弦樂器的發聲體以弦為主，來源載明琴身常見葫蘆共鳴器蒙皮，竹製琴頸穿過蒙皮；: For this kind of single-string instrument the string is the main sounding body; the sources record that the body commonly has a skin-covered gourd resonator with a bamboo neck passing through the skin; another type uses a wooden bowl as the resonator, covered with deerskin, with a bamboo strip entering from the side and the string passing over a bridge on the deerskin face. A further type has a drum-shaped body, a bamboo neck and bamboo pieces, a skin face, and strings running to wooden pegs at the side. The materials of the remaining strings and of some bridges and pegs are not stated.
演奏者將樂器直立，一手握住共鳴器上方的琴頸，以同手食指或指甲撥弦發聲；若邊舞邊奏: The player holds the instrument upright, grips the neck above the resonator with one hand, and plucks the string with the index finger or fingernail of that hand; when playing while dancing, the other hand supports the gourd resonator and shakes small bells. The sound is mostly a drone, and pressing the two sides of the neck slackens the string and lowers the pitch, the change being judged by ear, with no marks. A beginner first practises a steady grip, plucking with one finger and light pressure on the neck, then chooses among treble, middle and bass sizes; the two-string version is plucked the same way on both strings.
隨著時間演進，一弦琴逐漸從Baul民族的傳統表演藝術擴展到孟加拉地區的廣泛應用。: Over time the ektara spread from the Baul tradition's performance art into wider use across Bengal. Its single-string design later gave rise to the two-string dotara, showing how the instrument developed. During the Bangladeshi independence movement it became a symbol of national identity and cultural resistance, widely used in folk music and theatre.
